quote: Even hedonically, it is better to take one large loss than many small ones.
content: Fable grants the normative point, "the normative theory sides with the essay," and then correctly notes that the advice is needed because preference runs the other way. That is what the essay is for. One technical note: prospect theory's value function is convex for losses, and convexity is what makes one integrated loss hurt less than several separate ones (Thaler 1985). Preferences for splitting losses up also have a short horizon, such as sparing oneself two bad pieces of news in one evening. The essay's case, Enron and the author's own mistake, is a loss drawn out over years of partial concessions, each of which reopens the wound. On that scale, integration wins on the hedonic side as well.

quote: But there is less focus on speed, on giving up the fight as quickly as possible, integrating evidence efficiently so that it only takes a minimum of contrary evidence to destroy your cherished belief.
content: "A minimum of contrary evidence" means no more than the likelihood ratio warrants. That is proportionality, stated against the error the essay is correcting. For cherished beliefs that error is under-updating. Revising too little relative to Bayes, "conservatism," was among the first findings of the Bayesian-judgment research programme (Phillips & Edwards 1966), and belief perseverance after discrediting is its motivated form. Griffin and Tversky's over-reaction concerns vivid one-off signals, not the defence of long-held commitments. The essay's audience is the second group, as its opening makes clear: Traditional Rationality's arguer "will concede to contrary evidence eventually." The prescription is "integrating evidence efficiently." For a mind that drags its feet, the Bayesian speed is faster than its natural one.
